title: CR functions at CR singularities approximation, extension, and hulls

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Definition 3.1 begins, "We say:", but supplies none of the promised definitions. The immediately following prose repeatedly relies on four undefined notions: extension property, approximation property, fixed-neighborhood extension property, and fixed-neighborhood approximation property. Their precise quantifiers are essential to the later claims, so this is not merely stylistic; the document omits the definitions needed to interpret the results.

The text claims: "If M is contained in the Levi-flat hypersurface given by Im z_n = 0, then CR_H(M) does not have the fixed-neighborhood extension property as 1/(z_n-iε) is in CR_H(M) for all real ε ≠ 0." This is false without substantial additional assumptions on M. For example, for the zero-dimensional embedded submanifold M={0} (or for a submanifold on which z_n is identically zero), the restriction of 1/(z_n-iε) is the constant i/ε and therefore has an entire extension. Thus these functions do not disprove a fixed-neighborhood extension property for an arbitrary M contained in the stated Levi-flat hypersurface.

predicted_errors.error_location: Lemma 3.8, proof of closedness of SADH_q(X)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The purported proof that SADH_q(X) is closed starts: "suppose p_1 ∈ SADH_q(X). For any ε > 0 there is a p_2 ∈ SADH_q(X) that is within ε/2 of p_1." This assumes p_1 is already in the set, whereas to prove closedness one must begin with p_1 in its closure. The conclusion "p_1 ∈ SADH_q(X)" is therefore circular. Moreover, the asserted perturbation must preserve the strict monotonicity condition on ||φ_t(0)-q||, which is not justified. The lemma may be repairable, but the proof given does not establish it.

predicted_errors.error_location: Example 3.9, equation (5) and the claim that X is compact
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The construction is introduced as one "Given a compact set X," but the set in (5) contains only the slices z_3=1/k. It omits their z_3=0 accumulation set. For any boundary point z_1≠1 at which the assumed limiting boundary function is continuous, (z_1,φ_k(z_1),1/k) converges to (z_1,φ_∞(z_1),0), which is not in X as defined. Hence X is not closed and therefore not compact. The example cannot establish the stated claim about DH of a compact set without modifying X and rechecking the disc argument.

Equation (9) incorrectly replaces the strict condition Im z_2<0 from X_2 by Im z_2≤0 in the second component of DH(X). In particular, it asserts that points with 1<|z_1|≤2 and Im z_2=0 belong to DH(X). They cannot arise from a disc whose boundary lies in X_2, since X_2 excludes Im z_2=0; nor can they arise from X_1, because discs attached to X_1 have |z_1|≤1. Since the two pieces of X are disconnected, a boundary circle cannot mix them. The second term should retain a strict lower-half-circle condition (with only the |z_1|≤1 equality points supplied by the first term).

Example 3.11 states that "the only nonconstant attached analytic discs" are the displayed discs φ_n(ζ)=(n^{-1/2}ζ,1/n,1/n), and Example 3.12 consequently claims only finitely many attached discs when f has finitely many zeros. This is false as a statement about analytic discs. For every n and every nonconstant finite Blaschke product B, φ_{n,B}(ζ)=(n^{-1/2}B(ζ),1/n,1/n) is another attached analytic disc: on the boundary |B|=1, so both defining equations of M hold. There are infinitely many such parametrized discs even for a single zero of f. At most the examples have finitely/discretely many disc images or radii, which is materially different from the stated claim.
